paragraphs.text: This review explains a math tool for studying how brain cells, or neurons, combine the signals they receive. The tool is called partial information decomposition, or PID. It splits what two input neurons tell us about a third neuron into separate pieces.

It splits what two input neurons tell us about a third neuron into separate pieces.

paragraphs.text: Scientists still know little about how brains change sensory signals into useful behavior. Large recordings of many neurons now exist, but researchers need ways to turn that data into clear insights.

sentences.text: Scientists still know little about how brains change sensory signals into useful behavior.
Large recordings of many neurons now exist, but researchers need ways to turn that data into clear insights.

paragraphs.text: PID finds three kinds of information: redundant (shared by both inputs), unique (from one only), and synergistic (seen only in both together). In mouse brain tissue, tightly linked groups of well-connected neurons, called rich clubs, had 2.7 times more synergy than other groups. In monkeys, the share of redundant information rose sharply during reaching movements.

paragraphs.text: The main conclusion is that neurons do not just add up their inputs; they also respond to particular patterns. Still, PID shows patterns in the data, not the biological reasons behind them.

fuller.text: This review asks how groups of brain cells, or neurons, actually combine and transform information. It introduces a math tool called partial information decomposition, or PID, and shows how the authors and others have used it on recordings of real neurons.

fuller.text: The authors call understanding how brains process information a grand challenge of neuroscience. New tools can now record hundreds or thousands of neurons at once, but researchers still need ways to pull clear insights from that flood of data.

fuller.text: PID splits what several input neurons tell us about a target neuron into parts. Redundant information is what any one input could tell us, and unique information is what only one input tells us. Synergistic information appears only when inputs are seen together, so the authors treat it as a sign of real computation.

fuller.text: In mouse brain tissue grown in a dish, tightly linked hubs called rich clubs had 2.7 times more synergy than other neuron groups. Groups with more links between the input neurons had up to 50% more synergy. In monkeys, redundancy rose sharply during reaching movements, perhaps to send the move signal reliably.

brief.text: This review explains a math method for studying how brain cells handle information. How brains turn incoming signals into useful behavior is a grand challenge in brain science. The method splits what a cell learns from its inputs into parts, including "synergy." Synergy is information that only appears when several inputs are looked at together.

Synergy is information that only appears when several inputs are looked at together.

brief.text: In studies of mouse brain tissue and monkeys, synergy turned up all over brain circuits. In mouse brain tissue, groups of the best-connected cells had about 2.7 times more synergy. The authors conclude that cells do not just add up their inputs but respond to their patterns.
